newsitem.title: republic of Ireland: French, Dutch rift widens on banker's job prospects.
newsitem.headline: French, Dutch rift widens on banker's job prospects.

text.p: A bitter row between France and the Netherlands over liberal Dutch drug laws spread to monetary issues on Friday when France said that a Dutchman should not automatically head up Europe's planned central bank.
European Union leaders at a summit in the Irish capital confirmed Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg as the next president of the EU's European Monetary Institute (EMI) from July 1, 1997.

The EMI is the forerunner of the European Central Bank, which is due to run monetary policy after economic and monetary union (EMU) is launched in 1999. Duisenberg, Europe's longest-serving central bank chief, was widely tipped to head the ECB and oversee the birth of the planned single currency.
But French President Jacques Chirac told fellow EU leaders that the choice of Duisenberg as EMI chief did not mean he would automatically head the new central bank.
"The decision on the nomination does not prejudge the presidency of the European Central Bank," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told a news briefing.
"We will be in a new phase and no doubt there will have to be a new team and new personalities."
A Duisenberg snub would be a cruel blow to Dutch morale. Several Dutch candidates have missed out on high-profile international posts in recent years.

In a muted reaction, a Dutch diplomat said the Netherlands had never assumed that Duisenberg would automatically move from the EMI to head up the ECB. "We never drew any conclusions from his appointment," he said.
One EU source said there could be several candidates for the post of ECB chief.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet has long been believed to be interested in heading the ECB, but it is unclear how much support he has with Chirac.
Duisenberg, 61, has steered the Netherlands to successive years of growth and strong money and the Dutch economy is widely seen as a model for Europe's economic future.

The latest Dutch candidate to miss out on a major international post was former Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers, who was almost assured of taking over as NATO Secretary-General last year until Washington intervened and vetoed his candidacy.

Ten years ago former Dutch finance minister Onno Ruding was overlooked as managing director of the International Monetary Fund and, in 1990, he failed to land the presidency of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
One-time Dutch agriculture minister Gerrit Braks' bid to become director-general of the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organisation also ended in failure.
The nation even lost out when Frankfurt beat off Amsterdam's challenge to host the European Monetary Institute.
As consolation, The Hague was given Europe's anti-crime centre Europol, despite a vociferous campaign by the French who decry the Netherlands' policy of tolerating soft drug use.
The drugs row simmered on at Dublin, threatening to overshadow The Hague's preparations to assume the EU presidency in January.

Privately the Dutch fear their presidency -- aimed at promoting European unity -- could be bogged down in endless rows over how to combat the drug threat, hampering progress on weightier issues facing the 15-member bloc.
Drugs are illegal in the Netherlands, but sales of modest amounts of soft drugs from "coffee-shops" are allowed under a progressive 20-year drugs experiment.
France argues that this policy attracts drug "tourists", youngsters who visit the Netherlands to buy cheap and readily available narcotics.
